title: The constant angle of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod spirals is about 80°–85°

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The constant angle of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod spirals is about 80°–85°

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is about 80° in Nautilus, where each whorl is about three times as broad as its predecessor, and in ordinary ammonitoid and typical spiral gastropod shells is seldom below 80° and usually between 80° and 85°.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: \alpha \approx 80^\circ in Nautilus (b_{n+1}/b_n \approx 3); usually 80^\circ \le \alpha \le 85^\circ in ammonitoid and gastropod shells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the constant angle is in the neighbourhood of 80°; and hence also that, in all the ordinary Ammonitoid shells, and in all the typically spiral shells of the Gastropods, the constant angle is also a large one, being very seldom less than 80°, and usually between 80° and 85°.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions

fields.label: Finding

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit logarithmic spirals to shell whorls and estimate constant angles with uncertainty for Nautilus, ammonitoids and gastropods. Test Nautilus against about 80 degrees and estimate the fraction of ordinary taxa inside 80–85 degrees or below 80 degrees.

fields.value: The numerical band is unambiguous and is estimated from the same whorl measurements that test geometric expansion. Public images and scans cover Nautilus and a wide range of ammonoids and gastropods at a sample size that can reject an 80 to 85 degree norm. The calculation is standard once outlines are digitized.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate the logarithmic-spiral constant angle for Nautilus, ammonoids and typical spiral gastropods. A Nautilus angle near 80 degrees, and a distribution for the other shells seldom below 80 and usually 80 to 85 degrees, supports the claim; a substantially lower or broader distribution refutes it.

fields.value:

What counts as a typical spiral gastropod has to be fixed before the 80 to 85 degree band is tested.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If whorl breadths (equivalently conch diameters one revolution apart) expand by a factor r per whorl, the constant angle is alpha = arccot(ln r / 2 pi) (Thompson's own table: r = 1.5 -> 86.3 deg, 2.0 -> 83.7 deg, 2.5 -> 81.7 deg, 3.0 -> 80.1 deg, 3.5 -> 78.7 deg). The claim then predicts: Nautilus r about 3, alpha about 80 deg; for ordinary ammonoids and typically spiral gastropods alpha is usually between 80 and 85 deg (r between 1.72 and 3.00) and very seldom below 80 deg (r > 3.00).

fields.label: Method
fields.value: fetch.py obtains the files (Dryad downloads sit behind a browser proof-of-work challenge; they were fetched with headless Chrome and checksummed) and writes derived tables (committed). analysis.py computes, per Nautilus specimen, the median of dm[i]/dm[i-8] over the 45-degree stations (one revolution; all stations are post-hatching, first dm 18-27 mm); per ammonoid species, the median of dm[n]/dm[n-1] over half-whorl stations with dm >= 5 mm; per gastropod specimen, the median of r[k+2]/r[k] where r is the perpendicular distance of each digitised aperture's centroid from the coiling axis (apertures 180 deg apart; replicate digitisations pooled), then the median per species. Each r is converted to alpha = arccot(ln r / 2 pi) and the pre-registered band fractions are evaluated.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. (a) Nautilus pompilius: per specimen, the median whorl expansion rate WER (Korn's definition, (dm1/dm2)^2 over half a whorl, which equals the per-revolution diameter ratio r) over all measured post-embryonic stages; the median across specimens, converted to alpha, must lie in [78, 82] deg (r in 2.6-3.5). (b) Ammonoids: per species, the median WER over measured stages with conch diameter >= 5 mm (excluding the embryonic ammonitella), converted to alpha; at least 50% of species must have alpha in [80, 85] deg and at most 10% alpha < 80 deg. (c) Gastropods: per specimen (then averaged per species), the fitted per-revolution whorl expansion rate W from the Collins et al. 2021 helicospiral fits, converted to alpha the same way; at least 50% of species in [80, 85] deg and at most 10% below 80 deg. All three of (a), (b), (c) must hold for 'supports'.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if the Nautilus median alpha is outside [76, 84] deg, or if in either the ammonoid or the gastropod sample fewer than 40% of species fall in [80, 85] deg, or more than 20% fall below 80 deg. Anything between the pass and fail thresholds is 'mixed'. If the gastropod expansion parameter cannot be mapped to a per-revolution ratio from the dataset's documentation, part (c) is reported as not operationalizable and the verdict rests on (a) and (b) with a caveat.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: degrees, median constant angle of Nautilus pompilius (r = 2.87 per revolution)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson defines the constant angle through the per-whorl ratio of radii or whorl breadths, r = e^(2 pi cot alpha), and reads the angle off that ratio; the test therefore measures r and converts it with his own formula rather than fitting tangent angles to outlines. Modern 'whorl expansion rate' (Korn: WER = (dm1/dm2)^2 across half a whorl; Raup: W per revolution) is the same quantity for a planispiral shell. 'Ordinary ammonitoid shells' is operationalized as the species in a large published cross-section dataset (Devonian-Jurassic), 'typically spiral gastropods' as the 25 fossil and modern helicospiral species measured by Collins et al. 2021; neither sample was chosen by the tester. Deviation from the pre-registration: Collins et al. publish no per-revolution W (their W_e is a fitted rate of aperture-area increase), so r was computed directly from their raw digitised apertures (distance of the aperture centroid from the coiling axis at 180-degree steps, r = r[k+2]/r[k]), which is Thompson's own quantity; Nautilus r was likewise taken directly as dm[i]/dm[i-8] over the 45-degree stations rather than through WER.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Data from: Intraspecific variation in cephalopod conchs changes during ontogeny: perspectives from three-dimensional morphometry of Nautilus pompilius

Data from: Iterative ontogenetic development of ammonoid conch shapes from the Devonian through to the Jurassic (Walton & Korn)

Data associated with: Going round the twist - An empirical analysis of shell coiling in helicospiral gastropods

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The verdict follows the pre-registered rule, which fails because only 32% of ammonoid species (threshold 40%) and 46% of gastropod species fall inside 80-85 deg. The failure is one-sided: no ammonoid and no gastropod species, and only 5% of Nautilus, fall below 80 deg, so 'very seldom less than 80 deg' is strongly supported; the typical ammonoid and gastropod sits at 85-86 deg (r 1.5-1.7), just above Thompson's upper bound rather than inside it.

The Nautilus part of the claim ('in the neighbourhood of 80 deg', 'about three times') is confirmed closely: median 80.5 deg, r = 2.87, with very low scatter across 93 specimens and three populations.

The ammonoid sample (Walton & Korn 2018) was assembled to study pachyconic and globular conchs and is 82% Palaeozoic; globular Palaeozoic goniatites have low expansion rates, so it is probably biased towards high alpha relative to the Mesozoic ammonites Thompson likely had in mind (the 3 Jurassic and 6 of 11 Permian species are in band).

The gastropod sample is 26 species dominated by four struthiolariid/turritellid species from New Zealand and Australia; species were weighted equally, but it is not a random sample of 'typically spiral' gastropods. r for gastropods was measured on digitised apertures in a single sectioned plane (centroid distance from the axis), which is noisier than CT-based cephalopod diameters.

Per-species r is a median over ontogeny; whorl expansion drifts during growth (see thompson1917-ch11-08), so an adult-only or juvenile-only convention would move alpha by a fraction of a degree.

Sensitivity (not pre-registered, computed in a side check): the ammonoid in-band fraction is 0.26 with no size threshold, 0.32 at dm >= 5 mm (pre-registered), 0.29 at dm >= 10 mm, 0.26 at dm >= 20 mm, and 0.33 using only each species' last measured revolution; the median alpha stays at 85.5-85.6 deg and the below-80 fraction at 0 throughout, so the verdict does not depend on the threshold.
